analysis.title: European Utilities: US elections have potential repercussions for Utilities
key_insights: GS sees a 'Blue Sweep' after the US mid-term elections as likely positive overall for US renewable activities. Orsted and EDPR (and EDP) are named as the likely key near-term beneficiaries.
If US bond yields gradually normalise as election uncertainty abates, and datacenter infrastructure capex is redirected more towards Europe, GS would see this as a structural positive for RWE.
Any reduction in US bond yields would also benefit Iberdrola and National Grid.
A Blue Sweep is likely positive for wind manufacturers Vestas and Nordex, because the likelihood of onshore wind repowering could increase.

GS takes no view on how US fiscal policy might change. Bond yields have been a big overhang on the sector in recent months, driven by a focus on US government spending (deficit above 6% of GDP) and stickier inflation. Any change in policy or rhetoric could move rates and sector-relative performance. US yields declined 3 bp the day before the report.

GS takes no view on the outcome of the conflict affecting Hormuz. The energy crisis has put upward pressure on rates and raised investors' perception of regulatory risk for European Utilities (energy affordability). A Hormuz re-opening could lower the cost of capital in Europe and soften affordability concerns.

The main European developers in the US see a large onshore wind repowering opportunity, but approvals are not coming through yet because of regulatory hurdles. Faster permitting would likely benefit EDPR, RWE and Iberdrola, and would be a tailwind for Vestas and Nordex.

Democrats have historically asked for more regulation of AI and datacenter development. The pace of datacenter build-out could slow temporarily if regulatory requirements increase, though compute demand and adoption are unlikely to change.

When US local opposition rises, or equipment (CCGT) and grid-access waiting times grow, hyperscalers have been willing to redirect a larger share of datacenter investment to Europe. GS sees a possible acceleration in the European datacenter industry.

market_movers.rationale: Orsted is named as a likely key near-term beneficiary of a Blue Sweep for US renewables. Orsted has no US ticker in this report, so none is given.
EDPR (and EDP) are named as likely key near-term beneficiaries of a Blue Sweep for US renewables, and EDPR would benefit from faster onshore wind repowering permits.
RWE would see a structural positive if US yields normalise and datacenter capex shifts toward Europe, plus a benefit from faster US onshore wind repowering permits.
Iberdrola would benefit from lower US bond yields and from faster US onshore wind repowering permits.
National Grid would benefit from any reduction in US bond yields.
Vestas is a likely beneficiary because the likelihood of US onshore wind repowering could increase.
Nordex is a likely beneficiary because the likelihood of US onshore wind repowering could increase.

sector_views.rationale: A Blue Sweep is seen as likely positive overall for US renewable activities. Lower US yields and a Hormuz re-opening would also ease the cost of capital and affordability concerns.

macro_indicators.interpretation: Yields fell the day before the report. Further normalisation as election uncertainty abates would help Iberdrola, National Grid and RWE.
A focus on US government spending at this deficit level has been an overhang on bond yields and on the sector.

risk_factors: US bond yields may stay elevated because of the deficit above 6% of GDP and stickier inflation.
The energy crisis raises regulatory risk for European Utilities around energy affordability.
US onshore wind repowering approvals face regulatory hurdles and are not coming through yet.
Democratic-led regulation of AI and datacenters could temporarily slow US datacenter development.
geopolitical: Ongoing conflict affecting the Strait of Hormuz. A re-opening could lower the cost of capital in Europe and soften energy affordability concerns.
US mid-term election outcome, a 'Blue Sweep', and its implications for energy, AI and datacenter regulation.
